title: Welcome to Experimental Chemistry
content:
## 🔬 Welcome to Experimental Chemistry

::yellow[Experimental Chemistry] is the foundation of all chemistry work. It's where chemists design experiments, choose the right tools, and discover how to separate and purify substances.

### Why Does This Matter?

In real-world applications, chemists need to:
- **Measure** physical quantities accurately (mass, volume, temperature, time)
- **Separate** mixtures into pure substances
- **Purify** substances to ensure quality and safety
- **Identify** components in unknown mixtures

### Real-World Connection 🌍

In Singapore's pharmaceutical industry, companies must ensure medicines are pure before distribution. In food production, chemists separate and purify ingredients to meet safety standards. Even in environmental cleanup, separation techniques remove pollutants from water.

> 💡 **Key Insight:** The techniques you'll learn in this chapter are used daily in laboratories, factories, and research facilities around the world.

title: Measuring Physical Quantities: Time and Temperature
content:
## ⏱️ Measuring Physical Quantities

Chemists regularly measure four key physical quantities in experiments. Let's start with the first two.

### Time ⏱️

::yellow[Time] is measured in seconds (s), the SI unit for time.
- 60 seconds = 1 minute
- Measured using a ::blue[stopwatch]
- Used to track reaction rates, heating duration, and experimental timing

**Why it matters:** In reactions, timing is critical. A reaction that takes 10 seconds versus 100 seconds tells us how fast the reaction proceeds.

### Temperature 🌡️

::yellow[Temperature] measures how hot or cold something is.
- SI unit: ::purple[Kelvin (K)]
- Relationship to Celsius: ::purple[Temperature in K = Temperature in °C + 273]
- Measured using a ::blue[thermometer]

**Common temperatures:**
- Room temperature: 25°C = 298 K
- Boiling water: 100°C = 373 K
- Freezing point: 0°C = 273 K

> ⚠️ **Important:** Always convert to Kelvin when doing calculations in chemistry. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where all molecular motion stops.
speech_to_text_content: Measuring Physical Quantities. Chemists regularly measure four key physical quantities in experiments. Time is measured in seconds, the SI unit for time. 60 seconds equals 1 minute. Time is measured using a stopwatch and is used to track reaction rates, heating duration, and experimental timing. In reactions, timing is critical. A reaction that takes 10 seconds versus 100 seconds tells us how fast the reaction proceeds. Temperature measures how hot or cold something is. The SI unit is Kelvin. Temperature in Kelvin equals temperature in Celsius plus 273. Temperature is measured using a thermometer. Common temperatures include room temperature at 25 Celsius or 298 Kelvin, boiling water at 100 Celsius or 373 Kelvin, and freezing point at 0 Celsius or 273 Kelvin. Always convert to Kelvin when doing calculations in chemistry.

title: Measuring Physical Quantities: Length and Mass
content:
## 📏 Length and Mass Measurements

### Length 📐

::yellow[Length] is the distance between two points.
- SI unit: ::purple[metre (m)]
- Conversion: 1 kilometre = 1000 metres
- Measured with: ::blue[measuring tape, ruler]
- Used in experiments to measure dimensions of apparatus or reaction vessels

**Precision levels:**
- Ruler: accurate to nearest millimetre
- Measuring tape: suitable for larger distances

### Mass ⚖️

::yellow[Mass] is the amount of matter in an object.
- SI unit: ::purple[kilogram (kg)]
- Conversion: 1 kilogram = 1000 grams
- Measured with: ::blue[beam balance, electronic balance]

**Why mass matters in chemistry:**
- Determining amounts of reactants needed
- Calculating percentage yields in reactions
- Ensuring consistent experimental conditions

### Choosing the Right Balance

| Balance Type | Accuracy | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Beam Balance] | ±0.1 g | General lab use, less precise |
| ::yellow[Electronic Balance] | ±0.01 g or better | Precise measurements, small samples |

> 💡 **Key Point:** Always ::green[zero the balance before measuring] to ensure accurate results.
speech_to_text_content: Length and Mass Measurements. Length is the distance between two points. The SI unit is metre. 1 kilometre equals 1000 metres. Length is measured with measuring tape or ruler and is used in experiments to measure dimensions of apparatus or reaction vessels. A ruler is accurate to the nearest millimetre. Mass is the amount of matter in an object. The SI unit is kilogram. 1 kilogram equals 1000 grams. Mass is measured with beam balance or electronic balance. Mass matters in chemistry because chemists need to determine amounts of reactants needed, calculate percentage yields in reactions, and ensure consistent experimental conditions. A beam balance has accuracy of plus or minus 0.1 gram and is used for general lab use. An electronic balance has accuracy of plus or minus 0.01 gram or better and is used for precise measurements of small samples. Always zero the balance before measuring to ensure accurate results.

title: Measuring Volume: Apparatus and Accuracy
content:
## 📊 Measuring Volume

::yellow[Volume] is the amount of space a substance occupies.
- SI unit: ::purple[cubic metre (m³)]
- Common unit in labs: ::purple[millilitres (mL) or cubic centimetres (cm³)]
- Conversion: 1 cubic metre = 1,000,000 millilitres

### Apparatus for Measuring Volume

Different apparatus provide different levels of accuracy:

#### Pipette 🧪
- **Accuracy:** ±0.05 mL (very precise)
- **Fixed volume:** Typically 5-25 cm³
- **Use:** Transferring exact, small volumes of liquid
- **Advantage:** Delivers precise, fixed volumes

#### Volumetric Flask 🧫
- **Accuracy:** ±0.1 mL (very precise)
- **Volume range:** Up to 250 cm³
- **Use:** Preparing solutions of known concentration
- **Advantage:** Marks a specific volume with high accuracy

#### Measuring Cylinder 📏
- **Accuracy:** 1 decimal place (±1 mL for typical 50 cm³ cylinder)
- **Volume range:** 20-50 cm³
- **Use:** Measuring approximate volumes of liquids
- **Advantage:** Quick, general-purpose measurements

#### Burette 📍
- **Accuracy:** 2 decimal places (±0.05 mL)
- **Volume:** 50 cm³
- **Use:** Titrations, precise delivery of variable volumes
- **Advantage:** Measures changing volumes with high precision

### Gas Volume Measurement 💨

::yellow[Gas syringe] measures gas volumes accurately.
- Useful for gases produced in reactions
- Records volume changes during chemical reactions

> ⚠️ **Remember:** Choose apparatus based on required accuracy. Don't use a measuring cylinder when a pipette is needed for precision.

Common units in labs are millilitres or cubic centimetres. 1 cubic metre equals 1,000,000 millilitres. Different apparatus provide different levels of accuracy. A pipette has accuracy of plus or minus 0.05 millilitre with fixed volume typically 5 to 25 cubic centimetres. Pipettes are used for transferring exact, small volumes of liquid and deliver precise, fixed volumes. A volumetric flask has accuracy of plus or minus 0.1 millilitre with volume range up to 250 cubic centimetres. Volumetric flasks are used for preparing solutions of known concentration and mark a specific volume with high accuracy. A measuring cylinder has accuracy of 1 decimal place with volume range of 20 to 50 cubic centimetres. Measuring cylinders are used for measuring approximate volumes of liquids and provide quick, general-purpose measurements. A burette has accuracy of 2 decimal places with 50 cubic centimetre volume. Burettes are used for titrations and precise delivery of variable volumes. A gas syringe measures gas volumes accurately and is useful for gases produced in reactions. Choose apparatus based on required accuracy.

title: Gas Collection Methods: Water Displacement
content:
## 💨 Collecting Gases in Experiments

When reactions produce gases, chemists use specific collection methods depending on the gas properties. The choice depends on:
- Whether the gas dissolves in water
- The density of the gas compared to air

### Method 1: Water Displacement 💧

::yellow[Water displacement] collects gases by bubbling them through water into a gas jar.

**How it works:**
1. Gas is produced in the reaction vessel
2. Gas bubbles through water
3. Gas collects in an inverted gas jar above the water
4. Water level inside jar drops as gas fills the space

**Requirements:**
- Gas must be ::green[insoluble or only slightly soluble in water]
- Density of gas does NOT matter for this method
- Water density = 1 g/cm³

**Suitable gases:**
- ::green[Hydrogen (H₂)] - insoluble
- ::green[Oxygen (O₂)] - slightly soluble
- ::green[Nitrogen (N₂)] - insoluble
- ::green[Methane (CH₄)] - insoluble
- ::green[Carbon dioxide (CO₂)] - slightly soluble

**NOT suitable for:**
- ::red[Chlorine (Cl₂)] - very soluble
- ::red[Ammonia (NH₃)] - very soluble
- ::red[Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)] - very soluble
- ::red[Hydrogen chloride (HCl)] - very soluble

> 💡 **Why this works:** Water acts as a barrier. Only gases that don't dissolve in water can be collected this way. If the gas is soluble, it will dissolve into the water instead of collecting in the jar.
speech_to_text_content: Collecting Gases in Experiments. When reactions produce gases, chemists use specific collection methods depending on the gas properties. The choice depends on whether the gas dissolves in water and the density of the gas compared to air. Water displacement collects gases by bubbling them through water into a gas jar. Gas is produced in the reaction vessel, bubbles through water, and collects in an inverted gas jar above the water. The water level inside the jar drops as gas fills the space. The gas must be insoluble or only slightly soluble in water. The density of gas does not matter for this method. Water density equals 1 gram per cubic centimetre. Suitable gases include hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, methane, and carbon dioxide. Not suitable gases include chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and hydrogen chloride because they are very soluble. Water acts as a barrier. Only gases that don't dissolve in water can be collected this way.

title: Gas Collection Methods: Downward and Upward Delivery
content:
## 💨 Gas Density and Collection Methods

When a gas is soluble in water, we can't use water displacement. Instead, we use methods based on ::yellow[relative molecular mass (Mr)] and density.

### Understanding Gas Density

::yellow[Relative molecular mass (Mr)] = sum of all atomic masses in a molecule

- **Air has Mr = 29**
- Gases with Mr > 29 are **denser than air** (sink downward)
- Gases with Mr < 29 are **less dense than air** (float upward)

**Formula:** Density = mass ÷ volume

### Method 2: Downward Delivery ⬇️

Used for gases **denser than air** (Mr > 29)

**How it works:**
1. Gas is produced and flows downward (due to density)
2. Gas enters gas jar from the top
3. Gas sinks, displacing air upward and out
4. Gas collects at the bottom of the jar

**Key advantage:** Solubility in water doesn't matter

**Suitable gases (Mr > 29):**
- ::green[Chlorine (Cl₂), Mr = 71] - very soluble in water
- ::green[Hydrogen chloride (HCl), Mr = 36.5]
- ::green[Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), Mr = 64]
- ::green[Bromine vapour (Br₂), Mr = 160]

### Method 3: Upward Delivery ⬆️

Used for gases **less dense than air** (Mr < 29)

**How it works:**
1. Gas is produced and flows upward (due to low density)
2. Gas enters gas jar from the bottom
3. Gas floats, displacing air downward and out
4. Gas collects at the top of the jar

**Key advantage:** Solubility in water doesn't matter

**Suitable gases (Mr < 29):**
- ::green[Ammonia (NH₃), Mr = 17] - very soluble in water
- ::green[Methane (CH₄), Mr = 16]

### Comparison Table

| Method | Gas Property | Suitable For | NOT Suitable For |
|---|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Water Displacement] | Insoluble/slightly soluble in water | H₂, O₂, N₂, CO₂ | Cl₂, NH₃, SO₂, HCl |
| ::yellow[Downward Delivery] | Denser than air (Mr > 29) | Cl₂, SO₂, HCl | Less dense gases |
| ::yellow[Upward Delivery] | Less dense than air (Mr < 29) | NH₃, CH₄ | Denser gases |

> 💡 **Decision Guide:** First check if gas is soluble → use water displacement if insoluble. If soluble, check Mr → if Mr > 29 use downward delivery, if Mr < 29 use upward delivery.

Relative molecular mass equals the sum of all atomic masses in a molecule. Air has Mr of 29. Gases with Mr greater than 29 are denser than air and sink downward. Gases with Mr less than 29 are less dense than air and float upward. Density equals mass divided by volume. Downward delivery is used for gases denser than air with Mr greater than 29. Gas is produced and flows downward due to density. Gas enters gas jar from the top and sinks, displacing air upward and out. Gas collects at the bottom of the jar. The key advantage is that solubility in water does not matter. Suitable gases include chlorine with Mr 71, hydrogen chloride with Mr 36.5, sulfur dioxide with Mr 64, and bromine vapour with Mr 160. Upward delivery is used for gases less dense than air with Mr less than 29. Gas is produced and flows upward due to low density. Gas enters gas jar from the bottom and floats, displacing air downward and out. Gas collects at the top of the jar. Suitable gases include ammonia with Mr 17 and methane with Mr 16.

title: Drying Gases: Three Key Methods
content:
## 🌬️ Drying Gases in Experiments

Many gases produced in reactions contain water vapour. ::yellow[Drying agents] remove this moisture. Different drying agents work for different gases.

### Why Dry Gases? 💧
- Water vapour can affect reaction rates
- Moisture can cause unwanted side reactions
- Wet gases give inaccurate measurements
- Some applications require absolutely dry gases

### Method 1: Concentrated Sulfuric Acid 🧪

**Properties:**
- Works for ::green[most gases]
- Excellent water-absorbing capacity
- Very hygroscopic (attracts moisture strongly)

**How to use:**
- Bubble the moist gas through concentrated H₂SO₄
- Gas must pass through the liquid
- Moisture is absorbed into the sulfuric acid

**Limitations:**
- ::red[Cannot use with gases that react with H₂SO₄]
- Example: Cannot dry ammonia (NH₃) - it reacts with H₂SO₄

**Suitable for:** H₂, O₂, N₂, CO₂, Cl₂

### Method 2: Quicklime (Calcium Oxide, CaO) ⚪

**Properties:**
- Works for ::green[basic and neutral gases]
- Solid drying agent (not liquid)
- Readily absorbs moisture from air

**How to use:**
- Pass the moist gas through solid calcium oxide
- Gas must bubble through or pass over the solid
- Moisture is absorbed by the CaO

**Critical requirement:**
- ::red[Must be freshly heated before use]
- If left exposed to air, CaO absorbs moisture and becomes ineffective
- Heat it just before the experiment

**Limitations:**
- Cannot use with gases that react with calcium oxide
- Example: Cannot dry acidic gases like HCl

**Suitable for:** NH₃ (ammonia), other basic/neutral gases

### Method 3: Fused Calcium Chloride (CaCl₂) 🧂

**Properties:**
- "Fused" means the salt has been heated and dried
- Works for ::green[many common gases]
- Solid drying agent
- Also readily absorbs moisture from air

**How to use:**
- Pass the moist gas through solid fused CaCl₂
- Gas must bubble through or pass over the solid
- Moisture is absorbed by the CaCl₂

**Critical requirement:**
- ::red[Must be freshly heated before use]
- Calcium chloride absorbs moisture quickly from air
- Heat it just before the experiment to ensure effectiveness

**Limitations:**
- Cannot use with gases that react with calcium chloride

**Suitable for:** H₂, N₂, CO₂

### Comparison of Drying Agents

| Drying Agent | Form | How Gas Passes | Gases Dried | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Conc. H₂SO₄] | Liquid | Bubbles through | Most gases | Cannot dry gases that react with H₂SO₄ |
| ::yellow[CaO (Quicklime)] | Solid | Passes over/through | Basic & neutral | Must be freshly heated |
| ::yellow[Fused CaCl₂] | Solid | Passes over/through | H₂, N₂, CO₂ | Must be freshly heated |

> ⚠️ **Important:** Before choosing a drying agent, check if the gas reacts with it. If it does, choose a different agent. Always use freshly heated solid drying agents.
speech_to_text_content: Drying Gases in Experiments. Many gases produced in reactions contain water vapour. Drying agents remove this moisture. Different drying agents work for different gases. Drying gases is important because water vapour can affect reaction rates, moisture can cause unwanted side reactions, wet gases give inaccurate measurements, and some applications require absolutely dry gases. Concentrated sulfuric acid works for most gases and has excellent water-absorbing capacity. Bubble the moist gas through concentrated sulfuric acid. The gas must pass through the liquid and moisture is absorbed into the sulfuric acid. However, concentrated sulfuric acid cannot be used with gases that react with it, such as ammonia. It is suitable for hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and chlorine. Quicklime or calcium oxide works for basic and neutral gases. Pass the moist gas through solid calcium oxide. The gas must bubble through or pass over the solid and moisture is absorbed by the calcium oxide. Calcium oxide must be freshly heated before use because if left exposed to air, it absorbs moisture and becomes ineffective. It is suitable for ammonia and other basic or neutral gases but cannot dry acidic gases like hydrogen chloride. Fused calcium chloride is a solid drying agent that works for many common gases. Pass the moist gas through solid fused calcium chloride. The gas must bubble through or pass over the solid and moisture is absorbed by the calcium chloride. Fused calcium chloride must be freshly heated before use because it absorbs moisture quickly from air. It is suitable for hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide.

title: Check Your Understanding: Gas Collection Methods
content:
## Question 1: Selecting the Right Gas Collection Method

A chemist produces hydrogen gas (H₂) in a reaction. The hydrogen is slightly soluble in water and has a relative molecular mass of 2.

Which method should be used to collect the hydrogen gas?

A) Downward delivery
B) Upward delivery
C) Water displacement
D) Heating with concentrated sulfuric acid
speech_to_text_content: A chemist produces hydrogen gas in a reaction. The hydrogen is slightly soluble in water and has a relative molecular mass of 2. Which method should be used to collect the hydrogen gas? Option A: Downward delivery. Option B: Upward delivery. Option C: Water displacement. Option D: Heating with concentrated sulfuric acid.
explanation:
**Correct Answer: C) Water displacement**

**Why this is correct:**
Hydrogen gas (H₂) is ::green[insoluble or only slightly soluble in water]. Water displacement is the ideal method for collecting gases that don't dissolve in water. The hydrogen bubbles through water and collects in an inverted gas jar, where it remains because it doesn't dissolve.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- **A) Downward delivery** - This is used for gases denser than air (Mr > 29). Hydrogen has Mr = 2, making it much less dense than air. It would float upward, not downward.
- **B) Upward delivery** - While hydrogen is less dense than air, upward delivery is specifically used when the gas is soluble in water. Hydrogen is not soluble, so water displacement is the better choice.
- **D) Heating with concentrated sulfuric acid** - This is a drying method, not a collection method. It removes water vapour from gases, not for collecting them.

**Key principle:** When a gas is insoluble or only slightly soluble in water, always use ::yellow[water displacement] as the primary collection method, regardless of the gas's density.

title: Understanding Mixtures and Separation Principles
content:
## 🔀 What is a Mixture?

::yellow[A mixture] consists of two or more substances that are **not chemically combined**.

### Key Characteristics of Mixtures:

1. **Substances retain their properties** - Each component keeps its original characteristics
2. **No chemical bonds form** - The substances are physically mixed, not chemically bonded
3. **Can be separated** - The components can be separated using physical methods
4. **Variable composition** - The ratio of components can vary

### Examples of Mixtures:
- **Sand and iron filings** - Two solids
- **Salt water** - Solid dissolved in liquid
- **Oil and water** - Two immiscible liquids
- **Air** - Mixture of gases (N₂, O₂, Ar, CO₂)
- **Brass** - Mixture of copper and zinc metals

### Contrast with Pure Substances:

| Mixture | Pure Substance |
|---|---|
| Two or more substances | Single element or compound |
| Properties vary | Fixed, definite properties |
| Can be separated physically | Cannot be separated by physical means |
| Example: Salt water | Example: Distilled water (H₂O) |

## 🎯 How We Separate Mixtures

The separation method depends on the ::yellow[physical properties] of the substances involved:

### Physical Properties Used for Separation:

1. **Solubility** - How well a substance dissolves in a solvent
   - Salt is soluble in water; sand is not
   - Used for: Filtration, evaporation, crystallisation

2. **Boiling point** - Temperature at which liquid becomes gas
   - Different liquids boil at different temperatures
   - Used for: Distillation, fractional distillation

3. **Density** - Mass per unit volume
   - Different liquids have different densities
   - Used for: Separating funnel for immiscible liquids

4. **Particle size** - Physical dimensions of solid particles
   - Sand particles are larger than salt crystals
   - Used for: Sieving

5. **Magnetic properties** - Ability to be attracted by magnets
   - Iron is magnetic; most other metals are not
   - Used for: Magnetic separation

6. **Solubility in different solvents** - Different substances dissolve in different liquids
   - Used for: Chromatography

> 💡 **Decision Strategy:** Identify which physical property differs between the substances, then choose the separation method that exploits that difference.
speech_to_text_content: Understanding Mixtures and Separation Principles. A mixture consists of two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Key characteristics of mixtures include that substances retain their properties, no chemical bonds form, the components can be separated using physical methods, and the composition can vary. Examples of mixtures include sand and iron filings, salt water, oil and water, air, and brass. A mixture contains two or more substances while a pure substance is a single element or compound. Mixture properties vary while pure substance properties are fixed and definite. Mixtures can be separated physically while pure substances cannot be separated by physical means. The separation method depends on the physical properties of the substances involved. Physical properties used for separation include solubility, boiling point, density, particle size, magnetic properties, and solubility in different solvents. Solubility is how well a substance dissolves in a solvent. Boiling point is the temperature at which liquid becomes gas. Density is mass per unit volume. Particle size refers to physical dimensions of solid particles. Magnetic properties are the ability to be attracted by magnets. The decision strategy is to identify which physical property differs between the substances, then choose the separation method that exploits that difference.

title: Separating Solid-Solid Mixtures
content:
## 🧲 Separating Solid-Solid Mixtures

When you have two solids mixed together, the separation method depends on their different physical properties.

### Method 1: Magnetic Separation 🧲

**Principle:** ::yellow[Magnetic substances] can be separated from ::yellow[non-magnetic substances] using a magnet.

**How it works:**
1. Mix the two solids together
2. Pass a magnet over or through the mixture
3. Magnetic particles stick to the magnet
4. Non-magnetic particles fall away

**Magnetic substances:**
- ::green[Iron (Fe)]
- ::green[Cobalt (Co)]
- ::green[Nickel (Ni)]
- Some alloys (metal mixtures)

**Real-world application:** 🌍
Landfill waste is sorted using magnetic separation to recover valuable iron and steel from garbage.

**Example:** Separating iron filings from sand
- Iron filings are magnetic → attracted to magnet
- Sand is non-magnetic → not attracted to magnet
- Result: Clean separation of both materials

### Method 2: Sieving 🔍

**Principle:** ::yellow[Solids with different particle sizes] can be separated using a sieve.

**How it works:**
1. Place the mixture on a sieve with specific pore size
2. Shake or vibrate the sieve
3. Small particles pass through the pores
4. Large particles remain on top

**Why it works:**
- The pore size of the sieve acts as a barrier
- Large particles cannot fit through → remain on sieve
- Small particles fit through → fall below sieve
- Separation is based on particle size difference

**Example:** Separating gravel from sand
- Sand particles are small → pass through sieve
- Gravel particles are large → remain on sieve

**Real-world applications:** 🏗️
- Construction: Sorting aggregates by size
- Grain processing: Separating different grain sizes
- Flour production: Removing lumps

### Method 3: Using Suitable Solvents 💧

**Principle:** ::yellow[Solids with different solubility] in the same solvent can be separated.

**How it works:**
1. Choose a solvent where one solid dissolves but the other doesn't
2. Add the solvent to the mixture
3. One solid dissolves (becomes solute)
4. The other solid remains undissolved
5. Filter to separate:
   - ::green[Residue] = undissolved solid (remains on filter)
   - ::green[Filtrate] = solution with dissolved solid (passes through filter)

**Example:** Separating salt from sand
- **Solvent:** Water
- Salt dissolves in water → becomes solute
- Sand doesn't dissolve in water → remains as residue
- Filter to separate sand (residue) from salt solution (filtrate)

### Method 4: Sublimation 🌡️

**Principle:** ::yellow[Sublimation] is when a solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid.

**How it works:**
1. Heat the mixture gently
2. One substance sublimes (solid → gas)
3. The other substance remains solid
4. Cool the gas to collect the sublimed solid

**Substances that sublime:**
- ::green[Naphthalene] - used in mothballs
- ::green[Ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl)]
- ::green[Iodine (I₂)]

**Example:** Separating naphthalene from sand
- Heat the mixture
- Naphthalene sublimes → becomes gas
- Sand remains as solid
- Cool the naphthalene vapour → it condenses back to solid
- Sand and naphthalene are now separated

### Comparison of Solid-Solid Separation Methods

| Method | Property Used | Suitable For | Advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Magnetic separation] | Magnetism | Iron, cobalt, nickel | Quick, simple |
| ::yellow[Sieving] | Particle size | Different-sized solids | Effective, no waste |
| ::yellow[Suitable solvent] | Solubility | Soluble + insoluble solids | Works for many pairs |
| ::yellow[Sublimation] | Sublimation point | Substances that sublime | Recovers both solids |

> 💡 **Key Point:** Always identify which physical property differs between the solids, then choose the method that uses that property.
speech_to_text_content: Separating Solid-Solid Mixtures. When you have two solids mixed together, the separation method depends on their different physical properties. Magnetic separation uses the principle that magnetic substances can be separated from non-magnetic substances using a magnet. Pass a magnet over or through the mixture. Magnetic particles stick to the magnet and non-magnetic particles fall away. Magnetic substances include iron, cobalt, nickel, and some alloys. Landfill waste is sorted using magnetic separation to recover valuable iron and steel from garbage. Sieving uses the principle that solids with different particle sizes can be separated using a sieve. Place the mixture on a sieve with specific pore size and shake or vibrate the sieve. Small particles pass through the pores and large particles remain on top. Construction uses sieving to sort aggregates by size. Using suitable solvents uses the principle that solids with different solubility in the same solvent can be separated. Choose a solvent where one solid dissolves but the other does not. One solid dissolves and becomes solute while the other solid remains undissolved. Filter to separate the residue from the filtrate. Sublimation is when a solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid. Heat the mixture gently. One substance sublimes while the other substance remains solid. Cool the gas to collect the sublimed solid. Substances that sublime include naphthalene, ammonium chloride, and iodine.

title: Separating Solid-Liquid Mixtures: Filtration and Evaporation
content:
## 🧪 Separating Solid-Liquid Mixtures

When a solid and liquid are mixed, we use methods that exploit their different physical states.

### Method 1: Filtration 📄

**Principle:** ::yellow[Filtration] separates an ::yellow[insoluble solid] from a liquid.

**Key definitions:**
- ::yellow[Insoluble solid] = a solid that cannot dissolve in the liquid
- ::yellow[Filtrate] = the liquid that passes through the filter (the part we want)
- ::yellow[Residue] = the solid that remains on the filter paper

**How filtration works:**
1. Pour the mixture through filter paper in a funnel
2. Liquid (filtrate) passes through tiny pores in filter paper
3. Solid particles are too large to pass through → remain as residue
4. Collect the filtrate in a beaker below
5. The residue stays on the filter paper

**Why it works:**
- Filter paper has microscopic pores
- Liquid molecules are tiny → pass through pores
- Solid particles are larger → cannot pass through
- Physical separation based on particle size

**Real-world example:** 🌍
Filtering tea leaves from tea water
- Tea leaves (insoluble) → remain as residue
- Tea liquid (soluble) → passes through as filtrate

**Example in chemistry:** Separating sand from salt water
- Salt dissolves in water (soluble)
- Sand doesn't dissolve (insoluble)
- Filter the mixture:
  - ::green[Residue on filter] = sand
  - ::green[Filtrate] = salt water solution

### Method 2: Evaporation to Dryness 🔥

**Principle:** ::yellow[Evaporation] separates a ::yellow[dissolved solid] from its solvent.

**Key definitions:**
- ::yellow[Solution] = a homogeneous mixture where solute dissolves in solvent
- ::yellow[Solute] = the solid that dissolves (e.g., salt)
- ::yellow[Solvent] = the liquid that dissolves the solute (e.g., water)

**How evaporation works:**
1. Place the solution in an evaporating dish
2. Heat gently (using a Bunsen burner or hot plate)
3. Water evaporates (turns to steam and escapes)
4. Dissolved solid is left behind
5. Continue heating until all liquid is gone
6. Solid crystals remain in the dish

**Why it works:**
- Water has a much lower boiling point (100°C) than salt (doesn't have a single boiling point)
- When heated, water evaporates first
- Salt remains in the dish
- Eventually, all water is gone, leaving only solid

**Important consideration:** ⚠️
- Heat gently to avoid splattering
- If heated too quickly, hot liquid can splatter out
- Continue heating until no more steam appears

**Real-world example:** 🌍
Obtaining salt from seawater
- Seawater contains dissolved salt
- Heat the seawater
- Water evaporates
- Salt crystals remain in the pan
- This is how sea salt is harvested!

**Example in chemistry:** Obtaining salt crystals from salt solution
- Start with dissolved salt in water
- Heat in evaporating dish
- Water evaporates
- Salt crystals are left behind

### Comparison: Filtration vs. Evaporation

| ::yellow[Use when] | Solid is insoluble | Solid is dissolved |
| ::yellow[Mixture type] | Solid + liquid | Solution (dissolved solid) |
| ::yellow[What remains] | Solid residue on filter | Solid crystals in dish |
| ::yellow[What is lost] | Liquid (unless collected) | Liquid (evaporates) |
| ::yellow[Example] | Sand from water | Salt from salt water |

> 💡 **Key Decision:** If solid doesn't dissolve → use filtration. If solid is dissolved in liquid → use evaporation.

title: Crystallisation: Obtaining Pure Solid Crystals
content:
## 🔮 Crystallisation: Separating Pure Solids

::yellow[Crystallisation] separates a ::yellow[pure solid] from its saturated solution through a controlled cooling process.

### Key Concepts

**Saturated solution:** A solution in which ::green[no more solute can dissolve] at that temperature. The solution is "full" of dissolved particles.

**Why crystallisation matters:**
- Produces pure, well-formed crystals
- Better than evaporation for some substances
- Crystals are easier to handle and use
- Higher purity than direct evaporation

### The Crystallisation Process: Step-by-Step 📋

**Step 1: Create a Saturated Solution** 🔥
- Dissolve the solid in a hot solvent (usually water)
- Add solid until no more dissolves
- You now have a ::yellow[hot saturated solution]
- The solution is "full" - it can't hold any more dissolved solid

**Why hot?** At higher temperatures, solids are more soluble. You can dissolve more solid in hot water than cold water.

**Step 2: Cool Gradually** ❄️
- Allow the hot saturated solution to cool slowly
- As temperature decreases, solubility decreases
- The solution becomes ::yellow[supersaturated] (contains more dissolved solid than it can hold at the lower temperature)
- Dissolved solid begins to precipitate (come out of solution)
- Crystals start to form

**Why cool gradually?** 
- Slow cooling produces larger, better-formed crystals
- Fast cooling produces small, poorly-formed crystals
- Larger crystals are easier to separate and handle

**Step 3: Filter the Crystals** 📄
- Pour the cooled solution through filter paper
- Crystals remain as residue on the filter
- Remaining solution (mother liquor) passes through as filtrate

**Step 4: Wash the Crystals** 💧
- Rinse the crystals with a small amount of cold distilled water
- This removes any remaining impurities from the surface
- Use cold water so crystals don't redissolve

**Step 5: Dry the Crystals** 🌬️
- Place crystals on filter paper
- Allow to air dry or use gentle heat
- Crystals are now ready for use

### Visual Comparison: Evaporation vs. Crystallisation

| Step | Evaporation | Crystallisation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Heat solution | Heat solution |
| 2 | Continue heating | Cool gradually |
| 3 | All liquid evaporates | Crystals form from cooling |
| 4 | Solid left in dish | Filter to collect crystals |
| 5 | - | Wash and dry |

### Real-World Application 🌍

**Rock candy (sugar crystals):**
- Make a hot sugar solution
- Pour into jar and let cool slowly over days
- Large sugar crystals form as cooling occurs
- You can eat the crystals!

**Pharmaceutical industry:**
- Many medicines are purified using crystallisation
- Produces pure, uniform crystals
- Essential for drug quality and safety

### Advantages of Crystallisation Over Evaporation

✅ Produces larger, more uniform crystals
✅ Better control over crystal formation
✅ Easier to separate pure crystals
✅ Can wash away impurities
✅ Higher purity product

> 💡 **Key Principle:** Crystallisation exploits the fact that solubility changes with temperature. Hot solutions can hold more dissolved solid than cold solutions. As we cool, the excess solid has no choice but to come out of solution as crystals.

title: Distillation: Separating Liquids from Solutions
content:
## 🧬 Distillation: Separating Pure Solvents

::yellow[Simple distillation] separates a ::yellow[pure solvent (liquid)] from its solution.

### When to Use Distillation

Use distillation when:
- You want to separate a liquid from a solution
- The liquid and solid have very different boiling points
- You need to purify a liquid
- Example: Obtaining pure water from salt water

### How Simple Distillation Works 🔬

**The Basic Principle:**
- Different substances have different boiling points
- When you heat a solution, the liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first
- The vapour can be cooled and condensed back to liquid
- The dissolved solid stays behind in the flask

**Step-by-step process:**

1. **Heat the solution** 🔥
   - The liquid (solvent) evaporates first
   - Dissolved solid remains in the flask
   - Vapour rises into the condenser

2. **Cool the vapour** ❄️
   - Vapour passes through a condenser (cool water jacket)
   - Cold water cools the vapour
   - Vapour condenses back to liquid

3. **Collect the pure liquid** 💧
   - Condensed liquid drips into a collection flask
   - This is the pure solvent
   - Dissolved solid remains in the original flask

### Key Requirement: Boiling Point Difference ⚠️

**Simple distillation only works when there is a SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE in boiling points.**

**Example:** Salt water separation
- Water boils at 100°C
- Salt doesn't have a boiling point (it decomposes before boiling)
- Huge difference → distillation works perfectly!
- Water evaporates and is collected
- Salt remains in the flask

**Counter-example:** Separating two miscible liquids with similar boiling points
- If both liquids boil at similar temperatures
- Simple distillation won't separate them effectively
- Both liquids evaporate together
- You get a mixture instead of pure liquid
- Solution: Use fractional distillation (covered later)

### Apparatus Used in Distillation 🧪

A typical distillation setup includes:
- **Round-bottom flask** - contains the solution
- **Thermometer** - measures temperature (placed at side arm level)
- **Condenser** - cools and condenses vapour
- **Collection flask** - catches the pure liquid
- **Bunsen burner** - provides heat

### Real-World Applications 🌍

**Desalination (obtaining fresh water from seawater):**
- Many coastal countries use distillation
- Seawater is heated
- Pure water evaporates and is collected
- Salt remains behind
- Result: Fresh drinking water!

**Purifying liquids in industry:**
- Pharmaceutical companies distill solvents
- Chemical manufacturing uses distillation
- Water purification plants use distillation

### Why Distillation is Important

✅ Produces pure solvent
✅ Separates liquid from dissolved solids
✅ Useful for desalination
✅ Recovers valuable solvents
✅ Works with significant boiling point differences

> 💡 **Key Principle:** Distillation exploits boiling point differences. The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first, leaving solids behind. The vapour is then cooled and condensed to get pure liquid back.

title: Miscible and Immiscible Liquids
content:
## 💧 Understanding Liquid Mixtures

When two liquids are mixed, they can behave in two very different ways depending on their chemical properties.

### Miscible Liquids 🔄

::yellow[Miscible liquids] are liquids that form a ::yellow[uniform (homogeneous) solution] when mixed together.

**What happens:**
- The liquids completely dissolve into each other
- You get a single, clear phase (one layer)
- The liquids are completely mixed at the molecular level
- You cannot see where one liquid ends and the other begins

**Examples of miscible liquids:**
- **Water and ethanol** - mix completely
- **Water and glycerol** - mix completely
- **Acetone and water** - mix completely
- **Alcohol and water** - mix completely

**Why they mix:**
- Similar chemical properties
- Both are polar (or both non-polar)
- Molecules can "fit together" at the molecular level

**Visual:** 🔍
```
Before mixing:          After mixing:
Water | Ethanol    →   Uniform solution
(clear) | (clear)      (one layer, clear)
```

### Immiscible Liquids 🔀

::yellow[Immiscible liquids] are liquids that form a ::yellow[non-uniform (heterogeneous) mixture] when mixed together.

**What happens:**
- The liquids do NOT dissolve into each other
- Two separate layers form
- Each liquid remains distinct
- You can clearly see the boundary between the layers
- Layers separate by density (denser liquid sinks to bottom)

**Examples of immiscible liquids:**
- **Oil and water** - form two layers (oil on top, water below)
- **Petrol and water** - form two layers
- **Mercury and water** - form two layers
- **Benzene and water** - form two layers

**Why they don't mix:**
- Different chemical properties
- One is polar (water), one is non-polar (oil)
- "Oil and water don't mix" - famous phrase!
- Molecules cannot "fit together"

**Visual:** 🔍
```
Before mixing:          After mixing:
Oil | Water         →   Oil (top layer)
(clear) | (clear)       _______________
                        Water (bottom layer)
                        (two distinct layers)
```

### Density and Layer Arrangement 📊

When immiscible liquids are mixed, they separate into layers based on density:
- **Denser liquid** → sinks to bottom
- **Less dense liquid** → floats on top

**Example:** Oil and water
- Density of water ≈ 1.0 g/cm³
- Density of oil ≈ 0.9 g/cm³
- Water is denser → sinks to bottom
- Oil is less dense → floats on top

### Comparison Table

| Property | Miscible | Immiscible |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Appearance] | Single layer, uniform | Two layers, distinct |
| ::yellow[Mixing] | Complete dissolution | No mixing |
| ::yellow[Visibility] | Homogeneous solution | Heterogeneous mixture |
| ::yellow[Chemical similarity] | Similar properties | Different properties |
| ::yellow[Example] | Water + ethanol | Oil + water |
| ::yellow[Separation method] | Distillation | Separating funnel |

> 💡 **Key Insight:** The phrase "like oil and water" comes from the fact that these two liquids are immiscible. They refuse to mix, no matter how much you stir them. This is because water is polar and oil is non-polar, and they have fundamentally different chemical properties.

Both are polar or both are non-polar. Molecules can fit together at the molecular level. Immiscible liquids are liquids that form a non-uniform heterogeneous mixture when mixed together. The liquids do not dissolve into each other and two separate layers form. Each liquid remains distinct and you can clearly see the boundary between the layers. Examples of immiscible liquids include oil and water, petrol and water, mercury and water, and benzene and water. They do not mix because they have different chemical properties. One is polar and one is non-polar. Molecules cannot fit together. When immiscible liquids are mixed, they separate into layers based on density. The denser liquid sinks to the bottom and the less dense liquid floats on top. For oil and water, water is denser and sinks to the bottom and oil is less dense and floats on top. title: Separating Immiscible Liquids: The Separating Funnel
content:
## 🔀 Separating Immiscible Liquids

::yellow[A separating funnel] is used to separate ::yellow[immiscible liquids] (liquids that don't mix).

### How the Separating Funnel Works 🧫

**Basic principle:**
- Immiscible liquids form two separate layers
- Layers are arranged by density (denser at bottom, less dense at top)
- The tap at the bottom allows controlled removal of liquid
- Each liquid can be collected separately

**The process:**

1. **Pour the mixture into the funnel** 💧
   - The immiscible liquids separate into layers
   - Denser liquid sinks to the bottom
   - Less dense liquid floats on top

2. **Wait for complete separation** ⏱️
   - Allow time for layers to fully separate
   - A clear boundary forms between the layers
   - Don't shake or disturb the funnel

3. **Open the tap** 🔓
   - Turn the tap at the bottom slowly
   - Liquid begins to flow out
   - The bottom layer (denser liquid) comes out first

4. **Collect the bottom layer** 🧪
   - Place a flask below the tap
   - Let the denser liquid flow into the flask
   - Stop when you reach the boundary between layers

5. **Close the tap and change flask** 🔄
   - Close the tap to stop flow
   - Remove the first collection flask
   - Place a new flask below

6. **Collect the top layer** 🧪
   - Open the tap again
   - The less dense liquid flows into the new flask
   - You now have two separate, pure liquids

### Real-World Example: Oil and Water 🛢️💧

**Scenario:** Separating crude oil from water (common in oil refineries)

1. Oil and water are immiscible → form two layers
2. Water is denser (1.0 g/cm³) → sinks to bottom
3. Oil is less dense (0.9 g/cm³) → floats on top
4. Use separating funnel:
   - Open tap → water flows out (collected first)
   - Close tap, change flask
   - Open tap → oil flows out (collected second)
5. Result: Pure oil and pure water separated!

### Why the Separating Funnel is Ideal

✅ Works for ANY immiscible liquids (regardless of solubility in water)
✅ Both liquids are recovered pure
✅ Quick and efficient separation
✅ No heating required (unlike distillation)
✅ Simple to use
✅ No waste of materials

### Comparison: Separating Funnel vs. Distillation

| Aspect | Separating Funnel | Distillation |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Use for] | Immiscible liquids | Liquid from solution |
| ::yellow[Requirement] | Two separate layers | Boiling point difference |
| ::yellow[Heat needed?] | No | Yes |
| ::yellow[Speed] | Quick | Slower |
| ::yellow[Both recovered?] | Yes, both pure | Yes, pure liquid + residue |
| ::yellow[Example] | Oil + water | Salt water → pure water |

### Important Considerations ⚠️

**Do NOT use separating funnel for:**
- ::red[Miscible liquids] - they won't separate into layers
- ::red[Solutions] - the dissolved solid stays in solution
- ::red[Emulsions] - mixtures where liquids are finely dispersed

**Always:**
- ✅ Allow complete separation before opening tap
- ✅ Open tap slowly for controlled flow
- ✅ Collect each layer into separate flasks
- ✅ Stop at the boundary between layers

> 💡 **Key Principle:** The separating funnel uses the fact that immiscible liquids form distinct layers. By opening the tap, you can remove one layer completely, then remove the other. Each liquid is collected pure and separate from the other.

title: Fractional Distillation: Separating Miscible Liquids
content:
## 🔬 Fractional Distillation: Advanced Separation

::yellow[Fractional distillation] separates ::yellow[miscible liquids] that have ::yellow[similar boiling points].

### When Simple Distillation Fails ❌

**Problem:** What if you have two miscible liquids with similar boiling points?
- Example: Ethanol (boiling point 78°C) and water (boiling point 100°C)
- The difference is only 22°C
- When you heat the mixture, both liquids evaporate together
- You get a mixture of both vapours, not pure liquid
- Simple distillation doesn't work!

**Solution:** Use ::yellow[fractional distillation]

### How Fractional Distillation Works 🔬

**The key difference:** A ::yellow[fractionating column] is added to the distillation apparatus.

**What's inside the fractionating column:**
- Small glass beads
- Glass wool
- Other small solid objects
- These provide a LARGE SURFACE AREA for vapours to condense onto

**The principle:**
1. Heat the mixture of miscible liquids
2. Both liquids evaporate and enter the fractionating column
3. Vapours travel upward through the column
4. As they move up, they encounter cooler temperatures
5. The vapour with the HIGHER boiling point condenses first
6. The liquid with the lower boiling point continues upward
7. Eventually, the second liquid also condenses
8. Each liquid is collected separately at different temperatures

### Step-by-Step Process 📊

**Stage 1: Heating** 🔥
- The mixture is heated
- Both liquids evaporate
- Vapours enter the fractionating column

**Stage 2: Fractionation in the Column** 🌡️
- Vapours rise through the column
- The column is cooler at the top, warmer at the bottom
- Liquid with higher boiling point condenses lower in column
- Liquid with lower boiling point condenses higher in column
- Each liquid separates into different zones

**Stage 3: Collection** 🧪
- Liquid with higher boiling point condenses and flows out first
- Temperature rises as more of this liquid collects
- When temperature reaches the second liquid's boiling point, it starts to condense
- Liquid with lower boiling point is collected separately

### Real-World Application: Crude Oil Refining 🛢️

Fractional distillation is CRUCIAL in the petroleum industry!

**Crude oil contains:**
- Alkanes with different chain lengths
- Each has a different boiling point
- From short chains (low boiling point) to long chains (high boiling point)

**Products separated:**
- ::green[Petroleum gas] (boiling point < 25°C) - used for heating
- ::green[Petrol/Gasoline] (boiling point 40-200°C) - fuel for cars
- ::green[Kerosene] (boiling point 150-240°C) - jet fuel
- ::green[Diesel] (boiling point 200-350°C) - fuel for trucks
- ::green[Fuel oil] (boiling point 300-400°C) - heating oil
- ::green[Bitumen] (boiling point > 400°C) - road surfacing

**Why it's important:**
- Different products for different uses
- Maximizes value from crude oil
- Essential for modern society

### Comparison: Simple vs. Fractional Distillation

| Aspect | Simple Distillation | Fractional Distillation |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Use for] | Liquid from solution | Miscible liquids |
| ::yellow[Boiling point difference] | Large (>50°C) | Small (<50°C) |
| ::yellow[Apparatus] | Simple condenser | Fractionating column |
| ::yellow[Column contents] | None | Glass beads/wool |
| ::yellow[Separation quality] | Good for large differences | Excellent for small differences |
| ::yellow[Example] | Salt water → water | Ethanol + water |
| ::yellow[Industry use] | Water purification | Oil refining |

### Why the Fractionating Column is Essential 🔑

**Without fractionating column:**
- Both vapours condense at similar temperatures
- You get a mixture, not pure liquids

**With fractionating column:**
- Large surface area allows selective condensation
- Liquid with higher boiling point condenses first
- Liquid with lower boiling point condenses later
- Two pure liquids are collected separately

> 💡 **Key Principle:** Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with similar boiling points. The column's large surface area allows vapours to condense selectively based on their boiling points, even when those boiling points are close together.

title: Paper Chromatography: Identifying Mixture Components
content:
## 🎨 Paper Chromatography: Separating and Identifying Substances

::yellow[Paper chromatography] is a technique to separate and identify components in mixtures, especially useful for coloured substances and dyes.

### What is Chromatography? 🔬

::yellow[Chromatography] separates substances based on their ::yellow[different solubility in a solvent].

**Key principle:**
- Different substances dissolve to different extents in a solvent
- When a solvent moves through paper, it carries dissolved substances with it
- Substances that dissolve more (more soluble) travel farther
- Substances that dissolve less (less soluble) don't travel as far
- Result: Separation of mixture components

### The Paper Chromatography Process 📋

**Step 1: Prepare the Paper** 📄
- Use a strip of filter paper or chromatography paper
- Draw a pencil line near the bottom (the ::yellow[baseline])
- Mark the baseline with a pencil (NOT pen - pen ink will dissolve!)
- This is where you'll place the sample

**Step 2: Apply the Sample** 🎯
- Place a small drop of the mixture on the baseline
- Use a pipette or capillary tube
- The sample should be at the edge of the paper, not in the middle
- Let it dry completely

**Step 3: Prepare the Solvent** 💧
- Pour solvent into a beaker or chromatography chamber
- The solvent level should be BELOW the baseline
- Don't submerge the baseline - just touch it

**Step 4: Place the Paper in Solvent** 🌊
- Stand the paper strip vertically in the solvent
- The baseline should be just above the solvent level
- The solvent will be absorbed by the paper (capillary action)
- The solvent travels UP the paper

**Step 5: Watch the Separation** 👀
- As solvent moves up, it carries the sample with it
- Different components travel at different speeds
- More soluble components travel farther
- Less soluble components don't travel as far
- Coloured components separate into different coloured bands

**Step 6: Mark the Solvent Front** 🎯
- When solvent reaches near the top of the paper, remove the paper
- Immediately mark where the solvent front reached (with pencil)
- This is the ::yellow[solvent front] - the furthest point the solvent travelled

**Step 7: Analyze the Results** 📊
- You now have a ::yellow[chromatogram] (the final pattern)
- Each coloured band represents one component
- The position of each band shows how soluble that component is

### Understanding the Chromatogram 📈

**Layout from bottom to top:**
```
Solvent front ← furthest point solvent reached
        ↑
    Band 3 (least soluble)
        ↑
    Band 2 (medium solubility)
        ↑
    Band 1 (most soluble)
        ↑
   Baseline ← where sample was placed
```

**What the positions mean:**
- ::green[Band closest to baseline] = least soluble (doesn't travel far)
- ::green[Band farthest from baseline] = most soluble (travels far)
- ::green[Multiple bands] = mixture contains multiple components
- ::green[Single band] = pure substance (only one component)

### The Rf Value: Measuring Component Position 📐

::yellow[Rf value] (retardation factor) = a number that describes how far a substance travels.

**Formula:**
$$R_f = \frac{\text{Distance moved by substance}}{\text{Distance moved by solvent front}}$$

**Calculating Rf:**
1. Measure distance from baseline to the center of each band
2. Measure distance from baseline to solvent front
3. Divide: Rf = distance of band ÷ distance of solvent front

**Example:**
- Band traveled 6 cm from baseline
- Solvent front traveled 10 cm from baseline
- Rf = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6

**Rf value range:**
- Rf is always between 0 and 1
- Rf = 0 means substance didn't move (insoluble)
- Rf = 1 means substance moved with solvent (very soluble)
- Rf = 0.5 means substance moved halfway

**Why Rf is useful:**
- Each substance has a characteristic Rf value for a given solvent
- You can compare with known substances
- If Rf matches a known substance, you've identified it!
- Different solvents give different Rf values

### Identifying Unknown Substances 🔍

**Method:**
1. Run chromatography on your unknown mixture
2. Calculate Rf values for each band
3. Run chromatography on known pure substances
4. Calculate their Rf values
5. Compare: If Rf values match, you've identified the component!

**Example:** Purple food colouring
- Purple food colouring appears as a mixture
- Run chromatography
- You might see bands for red dye, blue dye, yellow dye
- Each has a different Rf value
- Compare with known food dyes
- Identify which dyes are in the purple colouring

### Colourless Compounds: Using Locating Agents 🔬

**Problem:** What if the components are colourless?
- You won't see any bands
- The chromatography won't show anything

**Solution:** Use a ::yellow[locating agent]

**What locating agents do:**
- React with colourless compounds to make them visible
- Turn colourless bands into coloured bands
- Allow identification of colourless mixtures

**Examples of locating agents:**
- UV light - some substances fluoresce under UV
- Iodine vapour - reacts with many organic compounds
- Ninhydrin - reacts with amino acids to give purple colour

**Important note:** 
- Specific locating agents are not required for O-level knowledge
- You just need to understand WHY they're used
- They make colourless compounds visible

### Advantages of Paper Chromatography ✅

✅ Simple, inexpensive technique
✅ Works for coloured and colourless compounds
✅ Can identify components in mixtures
✅ Quick results
✅ Uses small amounts of sample
✅ Can compare with known substances
✅ Rf values help identify unknowns

### Real-World Applications 🌍

**Food industry:**
- Checking purity of food additives
- Detecting artificial colours
- Quality control

**Forensics:**
- Analyzing inks in documents
- Identifying dyes in fibres
- Detecting drugs

**Pharmaceutical industry:**
- Checking drug purity
- Identifying components
- Quality assurance

> 💡 **Key Principle:** Paper chromatography separates substances based on solubility differences. More soluble substances travel farther up the paper. By comparing Rf values with known substances, you can identify unknown components in a mixture.
speech_to_text_content: Paper Chromatography: Identifying Mixture Components. Paper chromatography is a technique to separate and identify components in mixtures, especially useful for coloured substances and dyes. Chromatography separates substances based on their different solubility in a solvent. Different substances dissolve to different extents in a solvent. When a solvent moves through paper, it carries dissolved substances with it. Substances that dissolve more travel farther. Substances that dissolve less do not travel as far. The paper chromatography process involves seven steps. Step 1: Prepare the paper by using a strip of filter paper and drawing a pencil line near the bottom called the baseline. Step 2: Apply the sample by placing a small drop of the mixture on the baseline using a pipette or capillary tube. Step 3: Prepare the solvent by pouring solvent into a beaker and ensuring the solvent level is below the baseline. Step 4: Place the paper in solvent by standing the paper strip vertically in the solvent with the baseline just above the solvent level. Step 5: Watch the separation as the solvent moves up and carries the sample with it. Step 6: Mark the solvent front by marking where the solvent front reached with pencil. Step 7: Analyze the results by examining the chromatogram. The Rf value is a number that describes how far a substance travels. Rf equals distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent front. Rf is always between 0 and 1. Rf of 0 means substance did not move. Rf of 1 means substance moved with solvent. Each substance has a characteristic Rf value for a given solvent. You can compare with known substances. If Rf values match, you have identified the component. For colourless compounds, use a locating agent to make them visible. Locating agents react with colourless compounds to make them visible. Examples include UV light, iodine vapour, and ninhydrin. Paper chromatography is used in the food industry for checking purity of food additives and detecting artificial colours. It is used in forensics for analyzing inks and identifying dyes. It is used in the pharmaceutical industry for checking drug purity.

title: Determining Purity: Melting Point and Boiling Point

## 🌡️ Assessing Purity Using Melting and Boiling Points

::yellow[Pure substances] have characteristic, fixed ::yellow[melting points] and ::yellow[boiling points]. We can use these to determine if a substance is pure.

### Why This Works: The Effect of Impurities 🔬

**Pure substance:**
- Melts at a specific, sharp temperature
- Boils at a specific, sharp temperature
- Example: Pure water melts at 0°C, boils at 100°C

**Impure substance (mixture or contaminated):**
- Melts over a RANGE of temperatures
- Boiling point is RAISED compared to pure substance
- Melting point is LOWERED compared to pure substance
- The more impurities, the larger the range

### Effect of Impurities on Melting Point 🧊

**Pure ice:**
- Melts at exactly 0°C
- Sharp, single melting point

**Ice with salt impurity:**
- Melts at a LOWER temperature (e.g., -2°C)
- Melting occurs over a RANGE (e.g., -2°C to 0°C)
- The more salt, the lower the melting point

**Why this happens:**
- Impurity particles interfere with crystal structure
- Requires less energy to break crystal structure
- Lower temperature needed to melt

### Effect of Impurities on Boiling Point 🌊

**Pure water:**
- Boils at exactly 100°C
- Sharp, single boiling point

**Salt water:**
- Boils at a HIGHER temperature (e.g., 102°C)
- Boiling occurs over a RANGE
- The more salt, the higher the boiling point

**Why this happens:**
- Impurity particles require more energy to overcome
- Requires higher temperature to make liquid boil
- Higher boiling point

### Summary: How Impurities Affect Phase Changes

| Property | Pure Substance | Impure Substance |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Melting point] | Fixed, sharp | LOWERED, range |
| ::yellow[Boiling point] | Fixed, sharp | RAISED, range |
| ::yellow[Appearance] | Single value | Range of values |
| ::yellow[Purity indicator] | Sharp change = pure | Broad range = impure |

### Practical Determination of Purity 🧪

**Method 1: Measuring Melting Point**

1. Heat the substance slowly
2. Record the temperature when it starts to melt
3. Record the temperature when it's completely melted
4. Compare with reference value:
   - If measured = reference → pure
   - If measured < reference or range → impure

**Method 2: Measuring Boiling Point**

1. Heat the liquid slowly
2. Record the temperature when it starts to boil
3. Record the temperature when boiling continues steadily
4. Compare with reference value:
   - If measured = reference → pure
   - If measured > reference or range → impure

### Interpreting Purity Data 📊

**Example 1: Substance A**
- Reference melting point: 80°C
- Measured melting point: 78-82°C (4°C range)
- **Conclusion:** Fairly pure (small range)

**Example 2: Substance B**
- Reference melting point: 80°C
- Measured melting point: 70-80°C (10°C range)
- **Conclusion:** Impure (large range)

**Example 3: Substance C**
- Reference boiling point: 100°C
- Measured boiling point: 100-101°C (1°C range)
- **Conclusion:** Very pure (very small range)

### Why This Matters in Real Life 🌍

**Pharmaceutical industry:**
- Medicines must be very pure
- Impurities can be harmful
- Melting point testing ensures quality
- Patients' safety depends on purity

**Chemical manufacturing:**
- Chemicals must meet purity standards
- Purity affects product quality
- Melting/boiling point testing is routine

**Food industry:**
- Food additives must be pure
- Impurities can be toxic
- Quality control uses purity testing

### Advantages of Melting/Boiling Point Testing ✅

✅ Simple, quick test
✅ Requires small sample
✅ Inexpensive
✅ Reliable indicator of purity
✅ Can identify substances (if reference data available)
✅ Useful for quality control

### Limitations ⚠️

⚠️ Only works for pure substances (not mixtures)
⚠️ Requires reference data for comparison
⚠️ Some impurities may not significantly change melting point
⚠️ Doesn't identify WHICH impurities are present
⚠️ Needs careful measurement for accuracy

> 💡 **Key Principle:** Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points. Any impurity causes the melting point to lower and boiling point to raise, creating a range instead of a sharp value. By comparing measured values with reference values, we can determine purity.

title: Importance of Purity in Everyday Products
content:
## 🏥 Why Purity Matters: Everyday Applications

::yellow[Pure substances] are essential in products we use every day. Impurities can be dangerous, ineffective, or even toxic.

### Medicines and Pharmaceuticals 💊

**Why purity is critical:**
- ::red[Impurities can cause serious side effects]
- Some impurities are toxic
- Patients depend on consistent, reliable dosages
- Wrong purity = wrong dose = potential harm

**Examples:**
- **Aspirin:** Must be pure to be effective and safe
  - Impurities could cause allergic reactions
  - Impurities might not dissolve properly
  - Dosage would be unreliable

- **Insulin:** For diabetics, purity is life-or-death
  - Even tiny impurities can affect blood sugar control
  - Impurities could trigger immune responses
  - Patients inject insulin daily - safety is paramount

- **Antibiotics:** Must be pure to kill bacteria effectively
  - Impurities reduce effectiveness
  - Could lead to antibiotic resistance
  - Patient might not recover from infection

**Real-world consequence:** 🌍
In 2008, contaminated heparin (blood thinner) killed 81 people worldwide because impurities weren't detected.

### Foodstuffs and Food Additives 🍕

**Why purity is critical:**
- People eat food every day
- Impurities accumulate in the body
- Some impurities are carcinogenic (cause cancer)
- Children are especially vulnerable

**Examples:**
- **Food colourings:** Must be pure
  - Impurities could be toxic
  - Some artificial colours have been banned due to impurities
  - Example: Tartrazine (Yellow 5) must be pure to be safe

- **Preservatives:** Must be pure
  - Sodium benzoate must be pure
  - Impurities could cause food poisoning
  - Could spoil food faster

- **Flavourings:** Must be pure
  - Vanilla extract must be pure
  - Impurities affect taste and safety

- **Salt (in food):** Must be pure
  - Table salt needs iodine added (but no other impurities)
  - Impurities could be toxic metals
  - Pure salt is essential for nutrition

**Real-world example:** 🌍
In 2020, contaminated spice shipments were recalled because impurities included pesticides and heavy metals.

### Cosmetics and Personal Care Products 💄

**Why purity is critical:**
- Applied directly to skin
- Some people have sensitive skin
- Impurities can cause allergic reactions
- Long-term use of impure products is risky

**Examples:**
- **Makeup:** Foundations, powders must be pure
  - Impurities could cause skin irritation
  - Could clog pores and cause acne
  - Heavy metal impurities are dangerous

- **Skincare products:** Moisturizers, cleansers
  - Impurities could cause rashes
  - Could damage skin barrier
  - Allergic reactions possible

- **Toothpaste:** Must be very pure
  - Ingested regularly (especially by children)
  - Fluoride must be at exact concentration
  - Impurities could be toxic

### Water for Drinking 💧

**Why purity is critical:**
- Humans need water to survive
- We drink it every day
- Impurities accumulate in organs
- Some impurities cause serious diseases

**Examples:**
- **Bacteria:** E. coli in water causes severe illness
- **Heavy metals:** Lead causes brain damage (especially in children)
- **Chemicals:** Pesticides cause cancer
- **Minerals:** Too much fluoride causes dental fluorosis

**Real-world example:** 🌍
In Flint, Michigan (USA), lead contamination in drinking water caused a public health crisis. Thousands of children had elevated lead levels.

### Industrial Chemicals 🏭

**Why purity is critical:**
- Used in manufacturing
- Impurities can ruin products
- Can cause dangerous reactions
- Expensive to fix contamination

**Examples:**
- **Sulfuric acid:** Used in battery manufacturing
  - Impurities can cause explosions
  - Reduces effectiveness
  - Could corrode equipment

- **Sodium hydroxide:** Used in soap making
  - Impurities could be dangerous
  - Could cause burns to workers
  - Affects product quality

### Testing for Purity: Quality Control 🧪

Companies use purity testing to:
- ✅ Ensure product safety
- ✅ Meet legal requirements
- ✅ Maintain consistent quality
- ✅ Protect consumers
- ✅ Avoid liability and lawsuits

**Methods used:**
- Melting point and boiling point testing
- Chromatography (identify components)
- Spectroscopy (chemical composition)
- Microbial testing (bacteria/fungi)
- Heavy metal testing

### Summary: The Stakes Are High 🎯

|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Medicine] | Side effects, ineffectiveness | ::red[Life-threatening] |
| ::yellow[Food] | Poisoning, cancer risk | ::red[Serious illness] |

| ::yellow[Cosmetics] | Skin damage, allergies | ::yellow[Harmful] |
| ::yellow[Industrial] | Explosions, contamination | ::red[Dangerous] |

> 💡 **Key Insight:** When chemists say "purity matters," they're not being pedantic. They're protecting you. Every pure substance you consume or use has been tested by chemists to ensure it won't harm you. This is why purity testing is one of the most important jobs in chemistry.

## Question 2: Choosing the Right Separation Method

A student has a mixture of sand and salt. The student wants to separate these two solids.

Which separation method would be most suitable?

A) Magnetic separation
B) Sieving
C) Adding water, filtering, then evaporating the filtrate
D) Sublimation
speech_to_text_content: A student has a mixture of sand and salt. The student wants to separate these two solids. Which separation method would be most suitable? Option A: Magnetic separation. Option B: Sieving. Option C: Adding water, filtering, then evaporating the filtrate. Option D: Sublimation.

options.option_text: Adding water, filtering, then evaporating the filtrate

explanation:
**Correct Answer: C) Adding water, filtering, then evaporating the filtrate**

**Why this is correct:**
This method exploits the different solubility of sand and salt in water:
1. Add water to the mixture
2. ::green[Salt dissolves in water] (soluble)
3. ::green[Sand does not dissolve] (insoluble)
4. Filter the mixture:
   - Residue on filter = sand (pure)
   - Filtrate = salt solution
5. Evaporate the filtrate:
   - Water evaporates
   - Salt crystals remain (pure)
6. Result: Both sand and salt are recovered pure!

**Why other options are wrong:**

- **A) Magnetic separation** - Neither sand nor salt is magnetic. This method only works for magnetic materials like iron. Sand and salt would not be separated.

- **B) Sieving** - While sand and salt particles might have slightly different sizes, sieving is not effective because salt crystals and sand particles overlap in size. Many salt crystals would pass through with sand, and some sand would remain with salt.

- **D) Sublimation** - Neither sand nor salt sublime at reasonable temperatures. Sublimation only works for substances like naphthalene, iodine, and ammonium chloride. Sand and salt would not separate using this method.

**Key principle:** The method works because it uses a physical property that differs greatly between the substances - their ::yellow[solubility in water]. This is a much more effective difference than particle size or magnetic properties.

title: Check Your Understanding: Rf Values in Chromatography
content:
## Question 3: Understanding Rf Values

A student performs paper chromatography on a mixture. The results show:
- Distance from baseline to band A: 4 cm
- Distance from baseline to solvent front: 10 cm

What is the Rf value for band A?

A) 0.4
B) 0.6
C) 1.4
D) 4
speech_to_text_content: A student performs paper chromatography on a mixture. The results show distance from baseline to band A is 4 centimetres and distance from baseline to solvent front is 10 centimetres. What is the Rf value for band A? Option A: 0.4. Option B: 0.6. Option C: 1.4. Option D: 4.
explanation:
**Correct Answer: A) 0.4**

**Calculation:**

::purple[Rf = Distance moved by substance ÷ Distance moved by solvent front]

$$R_f = \frac{4 \text{ cm}}{10 \text{ cm}} = 0.4$$

**Why this is correct:**
The Rf value formula divides the distance the substance travelled by the distance the solvent travelled. In this case:
- Band A travelled 4 cm from the baseline
- The solvent front travelled 10 cm from the baseline
- Rf = 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4

**Why other options are wrong:**

- **B) 0.6** - This would be if the band travelled 6 cm (10 ÷ 10 = 0.6 is incorrect; the correct calculation is 4 ÷ 10)

- **C) 1.4** - This is impossible. Rf values are always between 0 and 1. The band cannot travel farther than the solvent front, so Rf can never be greater than 1.

- **D) 4** - This is just the distance the band travelled. It's not the Rf value. You must divide by the solvent front distance to get Rf.

**Important principles:**
- ::yellow[Rf is always between 0 and 1]
- Rf = 0 means substance didn't move (insoluble)
- Rf = 1 means substance moved with solvent (very soluble)
- Rf = 0.4 means substance moved 40% as far as the solvent front
- Each substance has a characteristic Rf value for a given solvent
- You can use Rf values to identify unknown substances by comparing with known Rf values

title: Check Your Understanding: Purity and Melting Points
content:
## Question 4: Determining Purity from Melting Point Data

A student measures the melting point of a sample of naphthalene (a white solid).

Reference melting point for pure naphthalene: 80°C
Measured melting point: 75-80°C

What can the student conclude?

A) The sample is definitely pure
B) The sample contains some impurities
C) The sample is definitely impure
D) The melting point data is inconclusive
speech_to_text_content: A student measures the melting point of a sample of naphthalene. Reference melting point for pure naphthalene is 80 degrees Celsius. Measured melting point is 75 to 80 degrees Celsius. What can the student conclude? Option A: The sample is definitely pure. Option B: The sample contains some impurities. Option C: The sample is definitely impure. Option D: The melting point data is inconclusive.

options.option_text: The melting point data is inconclusive

explanation:
**Correct Answer: B) The sample contains some impurities**

**Analysis of the data:**

| Observation | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Reference melting point | 80°C (pure) |
| Measured melting point | 75-80°C (range) |
| Melting starts at | 75°C (below reference) |
| Melting range | 5°C wide (75-80°C) |

**Key observations:**

1. ::red[The melting point is LOWER than the reference value]
   - Pure naphthalene melts at exactly 80°C
   - This sample starts melting at 75°C
   - This indicates impurities are present

2. ::red[The melting occurs over a RANGE (75-80°C)]
   - Pure substances have a sharp melting point
   - A range indicates impurities
   - The wider the range, the more impurities

3. ::yellow[The sample is not pure]
   - The combination of lower melting point + range = impurities

**Why other options are wrong:**

- **A) The sample is definitely pure** - WRONG. A pure sample would melt at exactly 80°C with a sharp transition, not over a range of 75-80°C.

- **C) The sample is definitely impure** - PARTIALLY CORRECT in conclusion, but the wording "definitely impure" is too strong. The data clearly indicates impurities, so this is the right conclusion.

- **D) The melting point data is inconclusive** - WRONG. The data is conclusive. A range of 75-80°C compared to reference 80°C clearly indicates impurities.

**The correct answer is B** because:
- The measured melting point is LOWER than the reference
- The measured melting point occurs over a RANGE
- Both of these are signs of impurities
- Therefore, the sample contains some impurities

**General principle:**
- ::green[Pure substance] = melting at exactly reference value
- ::red[Impure substance] = melting below reference value and/or over a range
- The wider the range, the more impurities present

## 📚 Experimental Chemistry: Complete Summary

You've now learned all the key concepts in experimental chemistry. Let's review what you've mastered:

### 1️⃣ Measuring Physical Quantities 📏

**Four key measurements:**
- ::yellow[Time] - measured in seconds with a stopwatch
- ::yellow[Temperature] - measured in Kelvin (K) with a thermometer
- ::yellow[Mass] - measured in kilograms with a balance
- ::yellow[Volume] - measured in m³ or mL with appropriate apparatus (pipette, burette, measuring cylinder, volumetric flask, gas syringe)

**Key insight:** Choose apparatus based on required accuracy

### 2️⃣ Collecting and Drying Gases 💨

**Collection methods depend on:**
- Solubility in water
- Density compared to air

**Methods:**
- ::yellow[Water displacement] - for insoluble/slightly soluble gases
- ::yellow[Downward delivery] - for gases denser than air (Mr > 29)
- ::yellow[Upward delivery] - for gases less dense than air (Mr < 29)

**Drying agents:**
- ::yellow[Concentrated H₂SO₄] - for most gases
- ::yellow[Calcium oxide (CaO)] - for basic/neutral gases
- ::yellow[Fused CaCl₂] - for H₂, N₂, CO₂

### 3️⃣ Separating Solid-Solid Mixtures 🧲

| Method | Property Used | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ::yellow[Magnetic separation] | Magnetism | Iron from sand |
| ::yellow[Sieving] | Particle size | Gravel from sand |
| ::yellow[Suitable solvent] | Solubility | Salt from sand |
| ::yellow[Sublimation] | Sublimation point | Naphthalene from sand |

### 4️⃣ Separating Solid-Liquid Mixtures 🧪

- ::yellow[Filtration] - for insoluble solids in liquids
- ::yellow[Evaporation] - for dissolved solids in solutions
- ::yellow[Crystallisation] - for pure solid crystals from solutions

### 5️⃣ Separating Liquid-Liquid Mixtures 💧

**Miscible liquids** (mix completely):
- Use ::yellow[distillation] (simple or fractional)
- Separate based on boiling point differences

**Immiscible liquids** (don't mix):
- Use ::yellow[separating funnel]
- Separate based on density differences

### 6️⃣ Analyzing Mixtures: Paper Chromatography 🎨

**Principle:** Substances separate based on solubility differences

**Key concept:** ::yellow[Rf value] = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent

**Uses:**
- Separating mixture components
- Identifying substances (compare Rf with known values)
- Analyzing coloured mixtures
- Using locating agents for colourless compounds

### 7️⃣ Determining Purity 🌡️

**Method:** Compare melting point and/or boiling point with reference values

**Pure substance:**
- Sharp melting point at reference value
- Sharp boiling point at reference value

**Impure substance:**
- Melting point LOWERED and occurs over a RANGE
- Boiling point RAISED and occurs over a RANGE

### 8️⃣ Why Purity Matters 🏥

**Real-world importance:**
- ::red[Medicines] - impurities can be life-threatening
- ::red[Food] - impurities can cause poisoning
- ::red[Water] - impurities can cause disease
- ::red[Cosmetics] - impurities can cause allergies
- ::red[Industry] - impurities affect product quality

### Decision-Making Framework 🎯

**To choose a separation method:**

1. **Identify the mixture type:**
   - Solid-solid?
   - Solid-liquid?
   - Liquid-liquid?

2. **Identify the physical properties that differ:**
   - Magnetism?
   - Particle size?
   - Solubility?
   - Boiling point?
   - Density?

3. **Choose the method that uses that property:**
   - Different property → different method

4. **Consider practical factors:**
   - Safety
   - Cost
   - Time
   - Equipment available
   - Purity required

### Key Vocabulary Checklist ✅

- ::yellow[Mixture] - two or more substances not chemically combined
- ::yellow[Pure substance] - single element or compound
- ::yellow[Solution] - solute dissolved in solvent
- ::yellow[Soluble] - dissolves in solvent
- ::yellow[Insoluble] - doesn't dissolve in solvent
- ::yellow[Miscible] - liquids mix completely
- ::yellow[Immiscible] - liquids don't mix
- ::yellow[Residue] - solid remaining on filter
- ::yellow[Filtrate] - liquid passing through filter
- ::yellow[Rf value] - ratio of distances in chromatography
- ::yellow[Melting point] - temperature at which solid becomes liquid
- ::yellow[Boiling point] - temperature at which liquid becomes gas

### Experimental Chemistry in Your Life 🌍

Every day, chemists use these techniques to:
- ✅ Purify medicines you take
- ✅ Test food safety
- ✅ Purify drinking water
- ✅ Refine crude oil
- ✅ Manufacture chemicals
- ✅ Analyze forensic evidence
- ✅ Develop new materials

> 💡 **Final Insight:** Experimental chemistry is about asking "What's in this mixture?" and "How do I separate it?" These fundamental skills underpin all of chemistry and are essential for understanding the world around us.

Four key measurements are time measured in seconds, temperature measured in Kelvin, mass measured in kilograms, and volume measured in cubic metres or millilitres. Choose apparatus based on required accuracy. Collection methods for gases depend on solubility in water and density compared to air. Methods include water displacement for insoluble gases, downward delivery for gases denser than air, and upward delivery for gases less dense than air. Drying agents include concentrated sulfuric acid for most gases, calcium oxide for basic or neutral gases, and fused calcium chloride for hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide. For separating solid-solid mixtures, use magnetic separation for magnetism, sieving for particle size, suitable solvent for solubility, or sublimation for sublimation point. For separating solid-liquid mixtures, use filtration for insoluble solids, evaporation for dissolved solids, or crystallisation for pure solid crystals. For separating liquid-liquid mixtures, use distillation for miscible liquids or separating funnel for immiscible liquids. Paper chromatography separates substances based on solubility differences. Rf value equals distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent. To determine purity, compare melting point and boiling point with reference values. A pure substance has a sharp melting point at reference value while an impure substance has melting point lowered and occurring over a range. Purity matters in medicines, food, water, cosmetics, and industry. To choose a separation method, identify the mixture type, identify the physical properties that differ, choose the method that uses that property, and consider practical factors.
